content:
We need retrosynthesis route with 1 reaction (one step) to target SMILES: [CH2:1]=[C:2]([c:3]1[cH:4][cH:5][cH:6][cH:7][cH:8]1)[C@@H:9]1[CH2:10][CH2:11][CH2:12][C@@:13]1([OH:14])[C:15]([F:16])([F:17])([F:18]

Interpret: It's a bicyclic? Actually structure: an exocyclic alkene attached to aromatic phenyl and a cyclopentanol with CF3 group? Let's parse: CH2= C( phenyl )-CH (attached to cyclopentane ring with OH and CF3). So target is a carbonyl-ene product: formed from a ketone and an alkene intramolecularly. So retrosynthesis: break the C-O bond (the new OH) and break the C-C bond formed, revert to a ketone and an alkene.

Thus precursor would be a molecule with a carbonyl (ketone) and an alkene that can undergo carbonyl-ene to give product. Likely the precursor is a cyclopentanone with phenyl substituent and CF3? Actually the product has a tertiary carbon bearing CF3 and OH (from carbonyl). In carbonyl-ene, the carbonyl oxygen becomes OH on the allylic carbon, and the carbonyl carbon becomes attached to the alkene carbon (forming new C-C). So precursor likely is a cyclopentanone (or cyclopentane with carbonyl) attached to phenyl and CF3? Let's think: In product, the carbon bearing OH is also attached to CF3 and part of ring. That carbon originally was carbonyl carbon (C=O) in ketone. After ene, carbonyl O becomes OH on adjacent carbon? Wait carbonyl-ene: an alkene (ene) reacts with a carbonyl (enophile). The allylic hydrogen transfers to carbonyl oxygen, forming OH on the allylic carbon, and new C-C bond between alkene carbon and carbonyl carbon, while carbonyl becomes alcohol. So product has an alcohol at the former allylic position, and the carbonyl carbon becomes attached to alkene carbon (now saturated). So in product, the OH is on the allylic carbon (which originally was part of alkene). In our product, OH is on the carbon that is part of cyclopentane ring (C@@H1...). That carbon is attached to CF3 and part of ring. So that carbon likely was the allylic carbon originally part of an alkene. The carbonyl carbon is the adjacent carbon (C@13?) which now is attached to CF3 and part of ring? Actually the carbon bearing CF3 is C15 attached to CF3 groups, and also attached to C13 (the carbonyl carbon). In product, C13 is attached to OH? Wait C13 is [C@@:13]1([OH:14])... So C13 is the carbon bearing OH and part of ring. C15 is attached to CF3 groups. So C13 is the carbon bearing OH (the allylic carbon). C15 is carbon attached to CF3 and attached to C13 (the carbonyl carbon). So in precursor, C13 would be carbonyl carbon (C=O) and C15 would be alkene carbon? Actually the new C-C bond formed is between carbonyl carbon (C15) and alkene carbon (C13?). Wait carbonyl carbon becomes attached to alkene carbon (the one that loses H). So after reaction, carbonyl carbon is now sp3 attached to CF3 and to the allylic carbon (now bearing OH). So in product, C15 is carbonyl carbon (now attached to CF3 and to C13). C13 is allylic carbon bearing OH. So precursor: C15 is carbonyl (C=O) attached to CF3 and to C13 (which is part of alkene). C13 is part of alkene (C=C) with CH2 exocyclic? Actually the alkene is CH2= C( phenyl )-C13? The product has exocyclic double bond CH2= C( phenyl )-C13? The SMILES: [CH2]=[C]([c1ccccc1])[C@@H]1... So the double bond is between CH2 and C2 which is attached to phenyl and to C13 (the chiral carbon). So the alkene carbon (C2) is attached to phenyl and to C13. So in precursor, that alkene would be CH2= C( phenyl )-C15? Wait C13 is attached to C15 after reaction, but before reaction C13 is part of alkene, so C13 is the allylic carbon? Actually the allylic carbon is the one bearing H that transfers. In carbonyl-ene, the allylic hydrogen is on the carbon adjacent to the double bond (the allylic position). The double bond is between C1 and C2. The allylic carbon is C2? No, the allylic carbon is the carbon adjacent to the double bond, which is the carbon bearing the hydrogen that migrates. In typical ene reaction, the alkene (ene) has an allylic hydrogen on the carbon next to the double bond (the "ene" carbon). The carbonyl (enophile) attaches to the terminal carbon of the double bond, forming new sigma bond, and the allylic hydrogen moves to carbonyl oxygen. So the product has an OH on the allylic carbon (which was originally sp3). So in our product, the OH is on C13 which is sp3 attached to ring and CF3. That suggests C13 was the allylic carbon originally attached to the double bond. The double bond was between C1 (CH2) and C2 (attached to phenyl and C13). So C13 is attached to C2 (the internal alkene carbon). So in precursor, C13 is attached to C2 (sp2) and has a hydrogen that migrates. After reaction, C13 becomes sp3 with OH. So the carbonyl carbon (C15) attaches to C13 after reaction. So in precursor, C15 is carbonyl attached to CF3 and to C2? Wait carbonyl carbon attaches to C13 after reaction, but before reaction it is attached to C2? Actually the new C-C bond formed is between carbonyl carbon and the terminal alkene carbon (C1? or C2?). In ene, the carbonyl carbon bonds to the alkene carbon that is not bearing the migrating hydrogen (the "ene" carbon). The allylic carbon (bearing H) becomes OH. So the new bond is between carbonyl carbon and the alkene carbon (C2). So after reaction, C15 is attached to C2 (which is attached to phenyl and C13). In product, C15 is attached to C13, not C2. Wait product SMILES: CH2= C( phenyl ) [C@@H]1... The C@@H is C13 attached to ring and OH. The CF3 carbon C15 is attached to C13, not to C2. So maybe my mapping is off.

Let's maybe not overthink. The retrosynthetic step: break the C-O bond (OH to carbonyl) and break the C-C bond formed (between C13 and C15). The resulting precursor would have a carbonyl (ketone) at C15 and an alkene (C1=C2) with allylic hydrogen on C13? Actually C13 would be part of alkene as allylic carbon? Might be a cyclopentanone with exocyclic alkene? Let's propose precursor SMILES: C= C( c1ccccc1 )C(=O)C(F)(F)F attached to cyclopentane? Wait C13 is part of cyclopentane ring; after reaction, the ring is intact. The carbonyl likely is part of the ring (a cyclopentanone). So precursor could be a cyclopentanone with CF3 at carbonyl carbon, and an exocyclic alkene attached to that carbon? Actually carbonyl carbon is part of ring, so cyclopentanone with CF3 substituent on carbonyl carbon (i.e., trifluoroacetyl cyclopentanone?) Not typical.

Maybe easier: Use tool to search for template matching carbonyl-ene transformation. Use functional_groups_broken: ["ketones"], functional_groups_formed: ["alcohol"], bonds_broken: ["C=O","C=C"], bonds_formed: ["C-O","C-C"]. The earlier attempt gave error because "ketone" not valid; correct functional group is "ketones". Use that.
